questions.q: What is the range of the correlation coefficient (r) and what do the extreme values +1.0 and -1.0 indicate?
questions.a: The correlation coefficient *r* ranges from -1.0 to +1.0. A value of +1.0 indicates a perfect positive linear relationship (as X increases, Y increases proportionally). A value of -1.0 indicates a perfect negative linear relationship (as X increases, Y decreases proportionally). A wrong answer (e.g., "0 to 1" or "extremes mean causation") reveals the student confuses correlation with causation or misremembers the bidirectional range.

questions.q: Explain in your own words the difference between a positive correlation and a negative correlation. Give one real-life example of each.
questions.a: Positive correlation: both variables move in the *same* direction (e.g., height and weight — taller people tend to weigh more). Negative correlation: variables move in *opposite* directions (e.g., hours of sleep and daytime sleepiness — more sleep, less sleepiness). A wrong answer that swaps the definitions or gives causation examples (e.g., "studying causes marks, so positive") shows the student hasn't grasped the *co-variation* concept distinct from cause-effect.

questions.q: A researcher computes r = -0.82 between "daily social media usage (hours)" and "academic percentile" for 200 Class 11 students. Identify the two variables, state the direction and strength, and explain what prediction a teacher could make.
questions.a: Variables: X = daily social media usage (hours), Y = academic percentile. Direction: negative (as usage ↑, percentile ↓). Strength: strong (|0.82| > 0.7). Prediction: a student reporting 4 hours daily usage would likely have a lower percentile than one reporting 1 hour. A wrong answer that says "social media causes low grades" reveals the causation misconception; one that calls 0.82 "weak" reveals poor strength classification.

questions.q: Two studies report: Study A: r = +0.45 between variable P and Q. Study B: r = -0.78 between variable M and N. Which study shows a stronger relationship? Justify using absolute values.
questions.a: Study B shows a stronger relationship because |-0.78| = 0.78 > |+0.45| = 0.45. Strength depends on *absolute magnitude*, not sign. A wrong answer choosing Study A because "positive is stronger" or "0.78 is negative so weaker" reveals the student confuses direction with strength.

questions.q: A news headline reads: "Research proves eating breakfast causes higher IQ in children (r = +0.65)." Critique this claim using principles of correlational research.
questions.a: The claim is invalid. Correlational research *cannot* prove causation. The +0.65 only shows that breakfast-eating and IQ co-vary positively. Third variables (e.g., socioeconomic status, parental education, home routine) could explain both. An experiment manipulating breakfast (random assignment to breakfast/no-breakfast) would be needed for causation. A wrong answer accepting the headline shows failure to apply the core limitation.

questions.q: Design a mini correlational study: choose two measurable psychological/behavioural variables relevant to Class 11 students, state your expected correlation (sign and rough magnitude), and describe how you would collect paired data from 30 students.
questions.a: Example: X = "hours of self-study per week", Y = "monthly test average (%)". Expect moderate positive correlation (r ≈ +0.50). Collect via anonymous Google Form: two numerical questions, one week recall. Good answer shows: both variables are continuous/measurable, hypothesis is directional, sample size stated, method yields paired scores. Poor answer uses categorical variables (e.g., "favourite subject") or expects r = +1.0, revealing misunderstanding of variable types or real-world variability.
